title: Trump wants to eliminate birthright citizenship before the election
description_short: Trump wants to eliminate birthright citizenship before the election
description_medium: In the weeks before the November 2020 election, Donald Trump reportedly tried to persuade people around him that he should issue an executive order ending birthright citizenship. The proposal would deny citizenship to children born in the United States when their parents were not full citizens. The timeline’s account also says Trump was frustrated by Attorney General William Barr’s resistance to the legally questionable idea.
description_long: In the weeks before the 2020 election, Donald Trump tried to persuade people around him that he should sign an executive order ending birthright citizenship, according to the account summarized by Trump File and reporting it attributes to The New York Times. The proposed order would deny U.S. citizenship to children born in the country when their parents were not full citizens. The timeline says Trump privately resented Attorney General William Barr’s resistance to the proposal, which the cited reporting characterized as legally dubious. The entry further argues that the change could reach people born before 2020 and estimates that millions of voters might lose citizenship; those are the source’s assessment, not an enacted policy or a court ruling. No executive order was issued as part of the event described here. The episode is relevant as an attempt to use presidential authority to alter a constitutional rule shortly before voting, with possible effects on the legal status and political participation of people born in the United States. The supplied account does not describe a finalized order or establish how courts would have resolved such a challenge.

title: Trump names SmartBiz as first fintech to become bank
description_short: Trump names SmartBiz as first fintech to become bank
description_medium: On March 17, 2025, SmartBiz became the first fintech company in President Trump’s second term to receive regulatory approval to become a bank. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago approved its acquisition of Centrust Bank NA in Illinois. The report notes that fintech bank conversions are uncommon and discusses deregulation as a possible reason more approvals could follow.
description_long: On March 17, 2025, SmartBiz became the first financial technology company during Donald Trump’s second term to receive approval to become a bank, according to the account. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago approved SmartBiz’s acquisition of Centrust Bank NA, based in Northbrook, Illinois. The arrangement was an acquisition of an existing bank rather than a new bank charter, and the article notes that fintech companies rarely become banks. It identifies potential regulatory advantages as one possible incentive and quotes Michele Alt of Klaros Group predicting that more fintech approvals could follow under the administration’s deregulatory approach. Those points describe a forecast and a possible incentive; they do not establish that SmartBiz received improper treatment. The article also discusses past concerns involving other fintech lenders and pandemic relief loans, but those allegations concern separate companies and do not demonstrate misconduct by SmartBiz. The event therefore records a specific regulatory approval and the broader policy debate it prompted: how fintech firms enter banking, what oversight follows, and whether a changing regulatory climate will lead to more such transactions.

title: Trump Fires 4 Inspectors General in One Week — Retaliation for COVID Oversight
description_short: Trump Fires 4 Inspectors General in One Week — Retaliation for COVID Oversight
description_medium: During one week in April 2020, President Trump fired four inspectors general. Among them were a Pentagon watchdog assigned to lead oversight of the COVID relief package and the Health and Human Services watchdog, whose office had reported hospital supply shortages. The dismissals drew criticism that independent scrutiny was being weakened during an emergency involving major public spending and health care.
description_long: In a single week in April 2020, President Donald Trump removed four inspectors general, including the Pentagon inspector general selected to lead a congressional oversight panel for the roughly $2 trillion COVID relief package and the Health and Human Services inspector general whose office had issued a report about hospital shortages. Inspectors general investigate and report on problems within federal agencies, making their independence central to public oversight of spending and administration. The timing led Democrats and other critics to interpret the removals as retaliation against watchdogs whose work could embarrass the administration. The supplied account says the firings weakened scrutiny just as emergency funds and strained health systems required close review. It also says the actions conflicted with the spirit, if not the letter, of a law requiring advance notice to Congress; the source does not provide a judicial ruling that the firings were unlawful. The episode raised a practical accountability concern: removing senior watchdogs can disrupt investigations and reduce confidence that executive agencies will be examined independently. The available record identifies two of the affected offices by role but does not name all four inspectors general or detail the status of each investigation after the dismissals.

title: Trump: Putin sends Kirill Dmitriev to meet with Trump Campaign associate
description_short: Trump: Putin sends Kirill Dmitriev to meet with Trump Campaign associate
description_medium: On January 11, 2017, Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev and George Nader met Erik Prince in the Seychelles to discuss Russia’s interests with the incoming Trump administration. Nader said Prince attended on behalf of Steve Bannon, then a senior Trump campaign figure. The account places the meeting within efforts to connect Dmitriev with Trump transition officials and describes a proposed policy plan.
description_long: On January 11, 2017, Kirill Dmitriev, a confidant of Russian President Vladimir Putin, and George Nader met Erik Prince on a remote island in the Seychelles. The Trump File account says they discussed Russia’s wishes for the incoming Trump presidency and that Prince attended on behalf of Steve Bannon, then the Trump campaign manager and soon-to-be White House strategist. It says Putin had tasked Dmitriev with establishing contact with the Trump transition team. Through Nader, Dmitriev had tried to arrange meetings with Jared Kushner or Donald Trump Jr.; he also contacted Rick Gerson, described as a friend of Kushner. The account says Dmitriev and Gerson drafted a plan for ways a Trump administration could support Russian aims and that Dmitriev shared it with Putin before the Seychelles meeting. The gathering occurred while international executives were also on the island to meet Crown Prince Mohammed bin Zayed, a circumstance the source says provided cover for the participants. The meeting is evidence of an effort to discuss policy and build access, but the supplied account does not establish that the proposed plan was adopted or that the meeting itself produced a government decision.

title: Donald Trump calls in to Fox News, OANN, and Newsmax
description_short: Donald Trump calls in to Fox News, OANN, and Newsmax
description_medium: On February 17, 2021, Donald Trump called Newsmax, One America News, and Fox News after Rush Limbaugh’s death. He discussed Limbaugh and himself, recalled the Medal of Freedom ceremony, and repeated his false claim that he had won the 2020 election during a Newsmax appearance. Trump also disputed President Joe Biden’s comments about the vaccine distribution plan.
description_long: On February 17, 2021, the day Rush Limbaugh died, Donald Trump called into Newsmax, One America News, and Fox News, appearing twice on Fox, according to the timeline. He spoke about Limbaugh and himself, and told Fox that Limbaugh had known in advance that he would receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom during the 2020 State of the Union address. On Newsmax, Trump repeated the false claim that he had won the 2020 election and said people were suggesting he replace Limbaugh on conservative radio. Host Greg Kelly asked about President Joe Biden’s statement that there had been no vaccine distribution plan when Biden took office. Trump recast the point as Biden saying there was no vaccine and called him a liar. The interviews combined memorial coverage with Trump’s political messaging during the post-election period. His repeated election claim continued to challenge the legitimacy of the result, while the vaccine exchange showed how he used a question about federal planning to attack Biden. The record documents what Trump said in those appearances; it does not provide evidence for his election claim or resolve the dispute about the handoff of vaccine distribution.

title: Trump: Senate rubberstamps Trump's personal lawyer for lifetime appeals court appointment
description_short: Trump: Senate rubberstamps Trump's personal lawyer for lifetime appeals court appointment
description_medium: On July 29, 2025, the Senate confirmed Emil Bove to a lifetime seat on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit. Bove had previously served as Trump’s personal lawyer. The account says nearly all Republican senators supported him, while Senators Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins joined Democrats in opposing confirmation; the supplied excerpt does not complete its description of the objections.
description_long: On July 29, 2025, the Senate voted to confirm Emil Bove to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, a position with lifetime tenure. Bove had previously served as Donald Trump’s personal lawyer. The supplied account says the confirmation was supported by Republicans except Senators Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins, who joined the opposition. The excerpt provided for this entry ends before it explains the specific concerns raised about Bove, so this description does not characterize or endorse any unstated objection. The event is significant because an appeals court judges cases that reach the federal circuit and its members can serve for decades; a confirmation therefore shapes the judiciary well beyond the administration that nominated the judge. Bove’s prior professional relationship with Trump is relevant context for the appointment, while the recorded vote shows broad party alignment with two Republican exceptions. The source title describes the Senate’s action as a rubber stamp, but the facts supplied here establish the vote and Bove’s former role, not the merits of every criticism of his nomination. This record should be read as an account of the confirmation and its institutional stakes, not as a substitute for the missing detail about the confirmation debate.

title: Trump: New York Times calls out preferential treatment in Jeffrey Epstein case
description_short: Trump: New York Times calls out preferential treatment in Jeffrey Epstein case
description_medium: A September 3, 2006 New York Times report examined whether Jeffrey Epstein received preferential treatment in Florida after prosecutors pursued a lesser charge than the offenses police believed they could support. The article described criticism from Palm Beach’s police chief and local editorial coverage. The supplied account does not explain Donald Trump’s role in the case, despite the timeline title.
description_long: On September 3, 2006, The New York Times published an account of questions about how Florida prosecutors handled the Jeffrey Epstein case. Epstein had pleaded not guilty to soliciting prostitution, while Palm Beach police said they had probable cause for more serious charges involving alleged sexual offenses against minors. Rather than proceeding with those charges directly, the state attorney presented possible charges to a grand jury, which indicted Epstein on the lesser count. The Times reported that the approach was unusual in Florida outside capital cases. Palm Beach Police Chief Michael Reiter accused prosecutors of special treatment and asked State Attorney Barry Krischer to step aside. A Palm Beach Post editorial also questioned whether the system had favored a wealthy, well-connected defendant over young alleged victims. The article documents contemporaneous scrutiny of prosecutorial decisions and the disparity between the charges police said they could support and the charge ultimately brought. The supplied summary does not describe Donald Trump’s involvement in the 2006 case, despite his appearance in this timeline entry’s title and tag set; no connection should be inferred from this account alone.

title: Donald Trump fires Defense Secretary Mark Esper, threatens to fire more
description_short: Donald Trump fires Defense Secretary Mark Esper, threatens to fire more
description_medium: On November 9, 2020, Donald Trump announced that he had fired Defense Secretary Mark Esper, the fourth official he had fired or demoted since Election Day, according to the account. Christopher Miller became acting secretary. The entry says federal law called for the deputy secretary to take that role and reports that White House personnel chief John McEntee warned staff against seeking other jobs.
description_long: On November 9, 2020, Donald Trump announced that he had fired Mark Esper as secretary of defense. The timeline described this as the fourth government official Trump had fired or demoted since Election Day. Esper had been reported to be drafting a resignation letter, but he told Military Times he had not intended to quit. Christopher Miller, then director of the National Counterterrorism Center, became acting defense secretary. The account says federal law required the deputy secretary to assume the acting role after a resignation or removal and characterizes Miller’s appointment as unlawful; the Pentagon did not comment when asked about the issue. Separately, a senior administration official said John McEntee, head of the White House Presidential Personnel Office, had warned staff they would be fired if they looked for another job. The reports caused concern among administration employees facing the transition after Trump lost the election. Together, the firing and reported threat to staff underscored the uncertainty inside the executive branch during the post-election period. This description attributes the legal characterization and account of McEntee’s warning to the cited reporting rather than presenting either as a court finding.

title: Trump: FAA grants Elon Musk permission to launch 25 rockets a year
description_short: Trump: FAA grants Elon Musk permission to launch 25 rockets a year
description_medium: On May 6, 2025, the Federal Aviation Administration authorized SpaceX to launch and land rockets at its Starbase site in Texas up to 25 times annually, five times the previous limit. The Trump File account frames the increase amid concerns about federal treatment of Elon Musk’s businesses, but the supplied record does not detail the safety review or the evidence behind that broader claim.
description_long: On May 6, 2025, the Federal Aviation Administration granted SpaceX permission to launch and land rockets at its Starbase spaceport in Texas as many as 25 times per year, five times the previous allowance, according to the linked timeline entry. The decision expanded the permitted frequency of activity at a facility owned by Elon Musk’s company. Trump File presents the approval as part of a broader pattern in which the Trump administration was protecting Musk and his businesses while agencies that had criticized them underwent changes. The entry mentions matters including safety investigations of Tesla’s self-driving technology and alleged workplace safety violations at SpaceX, but it does not describe their outcomes or show that the FAA’s decision altered either matter. The concrete event recorded here is the increase in launch and landing permissions. Its wider significance depends on the basis for the FAA’s decision, the conditions attached to the authorization, and the agency’s oversight of operations; those details are not included in the supplied summary. The record therefore supports describing a major regulatory approval and the conflict-of-interest questions raised by Musk’s closeness to the administration, while leaving the administration’s motive and the permit’s safety effects unresolved.

title: Trump: The IRS gives Donald Trump a likely illegitimate $72.9 million tax refund
description_short: Trump: The IRS gives Donald Trump a likely illegitimate $72.9 million tax refund
description_medium: In 2010, Donald Trump received a $72.9 million federal income-tax refund, along with $21.2 million in state and local refunds, according to records described by The New York Times. The account says the federal refund covered taxes paid from 2005 through 2008 plus interest and followed large reported business losses. Trump later described the payment to his lawyer Michael Cohen.
description_long: Donald Trump received a federal income-tax refund totaling $72.9 million in 2010, plus $21.2 million in state and local refunds, according to confidential records described in The New York Times investigation cited by the timeline. The federal sum represented all federal income tax he had paid for 2005 through 2008, with interest. The account says Trump generated the refund by reporting substantial business losses, including $1.4 billion in losses from core businesses for 2008 and 2009, which tax rules had prevented him from using in earlier years. The legitimacy of the refund became part of a long-running, private dispute with the Internal Revenue Service. In 2019 testimony to Congress, Trump’s estranged personal lawyer Michael Cohen recalled Trump showing him a large Treasury check and expressing surprise that the government had returned so much money. The source says it is unclear whether the refund arrived as one check or across multiple payments over several years. The figures describe the reporting’s account of tax records; the supplied material does not include the outcome of the IRS audit or a final ruling on whether the refund was proper.
